## Why save commands? {data-timing="75"}

Today we will build and test a shell script together in VS Code.

When another 100 files arrive, you will not want to type the same recipe
100 times, and future-you will not remember what present-you typed.

::: {.big-question}
How will you repeat exactly the same steps?
:::

::: notes
Time: 00:00-01:15.

Ask for one or two suggestions. Connect “save the commands” with a recipe:
someone should be able to inspect it, follow it and improve it.
:::

## The workflow for today {data-timing="180"}

::: {.flow .workflow-box}
create → run → inspect → break deliberately → improve
:::

We will use one small converter as our running example:

::: {.flow}
tab-delimited file → `tabtocsv.sh` → comma-delimited file
:::

The converter is intentionally limited. That is useful: a small failure is easier
to see than a giant mysterious pipeline.

::: notes
Time: 01:15-04:15.

Explain that Bash coordinates commands; specialist programs do specialist work.
Python or R become better choices when the task needs substantial data analysis.
Tell students this is a live-coding lecture: keep VS Code and a terminal visible,
and pause at each checkpoint rather than advancing on a fixed clock.
:::

## Utilities you might actually keep {.smaller data-timing="75"}

{{< embed ../../notebooks/shell-scripting.ipynb#shell-utility-examples >}}

These are examples of suitable jobs, not scripts to copy blindly. Backup and
synchronisation scripts should begin with a dry run and disposable directories;
be explicit about which direction data moves before trusting them.

::: notes
Time: 10:15-11:30.

These are ordinary utilities that save time and reduce repeated manual work.
They are deliberately not analyses: each has one practical job.

## Why are these shell jobs? {data-timing="75"}

{{< embed ../../notebooks/shell-scripting.ipynb#shell-utility-fit >}}

::: notes
Time: 11:30-12:45.

Use the image converter as the key example: Bash chooses image paths and calls
a converter; it does not itself understand image pixels. Python or R are not
wrong alternatives—they are better when the task becomes an analysis.
:::

## Meet the boilerplate {.smaller data-timing="60"}

{{< embed ../../notebooks/shell-scripting.ipynb#shell-anatomy >}}

| Part | Question it answers |
|:--|:--|
| Shebang | Who should read the script? |
| Comments | What is this file? |
| Commands | What should happen? |
| Exit status | Did the script report success? |

::: notes
Time: 12:45-13:45.

“Boilerplate” means a starting pattern. Read the script once from top to bottom,
then unpack its four parts on the next slides.
:::

## Create `boilerplate.sh` in VS Code {data-timing="420"}

Create a new file called `boilerplate.sh` in `code/` and type this with me:

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Author: Your Name <your.login@your.email.domain>
# Script: boilerplate.sh
# Desc: Simple boilerplate for shell scripts
# Arguments: None
# Date: Month YYYY

printf '\nThis is a shell script!\n\n'
```

::: {.live-demo}
**Do this now:** create the file in the editor, save it, then compare your filename and first line.
:::

::: notes
Time: 13:45-20:45.

Create the file visibly in VS Code and let students type or paste it. Explain that
the `.sh` suffix helps people and editors recognise the file; the shebang matters
when the file is executed directly.
:::

## Who should read it? {data-timing="60"}

{{< embed ../../notebooks/shell-scripting.ipynb#shell-boilerplate-interpreter >}}

::: notes
Time: 20:45-21:45.

Pronounce `#!` as “hash-bang” if useful. The main idea is simply that this line
selects Bash when the file itself is executed.
:::

## Notes for people {data-timing="60"}

{{< embed ../../notebooks/shell-scripting.ipynb#shell-boilerplate-comments >}}

::: notes
Time: 21:45-22:45.

Good comments answer practical questions: who wrote this, what is it for, and
what input does it expect? Comments explain the recipe to its readers.
:::

## Commands do the work {data-timing="60"}

{{< embed ../../notebooks/shell-scripting.ipynb#shell-boilerplate-body >}}

::: notes
Time: 22:45-23:45.

The body can contain commands students already know. A script becomes useful by
putting those familiar commands in a deliberate order.
:::

## Report success or failure {data-timing="60"}

```bash
exit 0
```

`exit` stops the script and returns a status to whatever started it. By convention,
`0` means success; a nonzero value means that something went wrong.

::: {.plain-language}
`0` = “I finished successfully”<br>
nonzero = “Something went wrong”
:::

::: notes
Time: 23:45-24:45.

This is a message to the calling shell or program. It does not prove that the
scientific result is correct, and `exit 0` should not be used to hide failure.
:::

## Run the script {data-timing="60"}

{{< embed ../../notebooks/shell-scripting.ipynb#shell-run-bash >}}

Expected output:

```text
This is a shell script!
```

::: notes
Time: 24:45-25:45.

Keep this first run simple. Direct execution, permissions and PATH remain in the
chapter and practical material.
:::

## Execute it through the shebang {data-timing="300"}

Now make the file executable and run it directly:

```bash
chmod u+x code/boilerplate.sh
./code/boilerplate.sh
```

Here `./code/boilerplate.sh` means “start here, then look under `code/`”. The
current directory is not normally searched automatically for commands.

::: {.checkpoint}
**Checkpoint:** both invocation methods should print the same message.
:::

::: notes
Time: 25:45-30:45.

If direct execution fails, check `ls -l code/boilerplate.sh` and confirm that the
terminal is at the project root. Do not turn this into a PATH detour yet.
:::

## Add an explicit status {data-timing="240"}

Add this line to the bottom of the script:

```bash
exit 0
```

::: {.plain-language}
`0` = “I finished successfully”<br>
nonzero = “Something went wrong”
:::

Check the status immediately:

```bash
./code/boilerplate.sh
echo "$?"
```

`exit 0` reports success; it does not prove that a scientific result is correct.

## Recovery checkpoint {data-timing="180"}

If your file has drifted, recreate this minimum version in the editor:

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
printf 'This is a shell script!\n'
exit 0
```

Then save it as `boilerplate.sh` in `code/` and run:

```bash
bash -n code/boilerplate.sh
bash code/boilerplate.sh
```

`bash -n` checks syntax without running the script. It does not check whether
input files or external commands exist.

::: {.checkpoint}
**Checkpoint:** a syntax check passes and the script prints one line.
:::

::: notes
Time: 34:45-37:45.

Ask students to predict the status before running `echo "$?"`. Keep this as a
catch-up example, not a second exercise students must type from scratch.
:::

## Create disposable input data {data-timing="300"}

Before touching a converter, make data that can be destroyed without regret:

```bash
mkdir -p sandbox/shell-demo
printf 'species\tcount\noak\t12\n' > sandbox/shell-demo/test.txt
cat sandbox/shell-demo/test.txt
```

::: {.checkpoint}
**Checkpoint:** the input is under `sandbox/`, not inside `data/` or `results/`.
:::

::: notes
Time: 43:45-48:45.

Explain why disposable practice files matter. Students should not debug a converter by
experimenting on the only copy of assessed or irreplaceable data.
:::

## Build the first `tabtocsv.sh` {data-timing="420"}

Create `tabtocsv.sh` in `code/`:

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
echo "Creating a comma delimited version of $1 ..."
cat $1 | tr -s "\t" "," >> $1.csv
echo "Done!"
exit 0
```

Run it on the disposable input:

```bash
bash code/tabtocsv.sh sandbox/shell-demo/test.txt
cat sandbox/shell-demo/test.txt.csv
```

::: {.live-demo}
**Do this now:** run the starter once, inspect the output, and think about + discuss what the script assumes.
:::

::: notes
Time: 48:45-55:45.

Do not present this as a finished converter. The unquoted `$1`, squeezing `tr`,
append redirection and unconditional success are deliberate teaching problems.
:::

## A useful script has a clear job {data-timing="60"}

The practical starter `tabtocsv.sh` has one intended job:

::: {.flow .workflow-box}
tab-delimited file → `tabtocsv.sh` → comma-delimited file
:::

Before trusting it, ask:

- What input does it expect?
- Where will it put the result?
- What could make it fail?

The live demo shows the starter as it is, including its limitations. In the practical, you will improve it and save the result in `results/`; the notebook walks through that work.

::: notes
Time: 55:45-56:45.

Do not inspect every line of the starter here. Establish its intended input and
output first; students will investigate the implementation in the practical.
:::

## Break it deliberately: reruns {data-timing="300"}

Run the same command again:

```bash
bash code/tabtocsv.sh sandbox/shell-demo/test.txt
cat sandbox/shell-demo/test.txt.csv
```

Why are rows duplicated? `>>` appends instead of replacing the output.

::: {.live-demo}
**Pause:** predict the second output before running the command, then discuss your prediction.
:::

::: notes
Time: 56:45-61:45.

Use this to introduce the distinction between `>` and `>>`. The original input
should remain unchanged, while the generated output is deliberately not idempotent.
:::

## Running is not the same as being right {data-timing="90"}

{{< embed ../../notebooks/shell-scripting.ipynb#tabtocsv-empty-fields >}}

::: notes
Time: 61:45-63:15.

This is the key scientific warning. The command completes, but the missing value
vanishes. Successful execution and correct data are different claims.
:::

## Break it deliberately: a space in the path {data-timing="300"}

Make a copy with a space in its name:

```bash
cp sandbox/shell-demo/test.txt 'sandbox/shell-demo/field notes.txt'
bash code/tabtocsv.sh 'sandbox/shell-demo/field notes.txt'
echo "$?"
```

The caller quoted the path, but the script used `$1` without quotes internally.
Quoting must be correct at every use. This is a useful failure to fix in the
practical, not an argument for avoiding spaces in real filenames.

::: notes
Time: 63:15-68:15.

Let students observe the error and status. If the demonstration behaves slightly
differently across systems, focus on the principle: unquoted expansion can split
one path into multiple words.
:::

## The improvement checklist {data-timing="300"}

Before calling a script reliable, ask:

- Does it check the number of arguments?
- Does it check that the input exists and is readable?
- Are variables quoted when they should remain one value?
- Does it keep input and output distinct?
- Does it handle reruns deliberately?
- Does its exit status reflect failure?
- Have we inspected the output, not merely seen a zero status?

::: {.flow}
predict → test on disposable data → inspect → improve
:::

::: notes
Time: 68:15-73:15.

This is the bridge from demonstration to practical. Do not live-code every fix;
ask students to apply the checklist to the starter and compare approaches.
:::

## Practical: your next shell script {data-timing="420"}

::: {.flow}
predict → test on disposable data → inspect → improve
:::

Write `csvtospace.sh` to convert a comma-separated input to a space-separated output. Run it from the project root and pass one readable input path.

It must:

- leave the input unchanged and write `results/<input-filename>.txt` (for example, `1800.csv` produces `1800.csv.txt`),
- create `results/` if it does not exist and replace the generated output on reruns,
- preserve repeated commas as repeated spaces so empty fields are not silently removed,
- report missing, unreadable or invalid inputs to standard error and return a non-zero status, and
- state the limitations of simple delimiter substitution.

The supplied temperature CSVs do not contain quoted commas. This is not a general CSV parser: quoted commas are data, and fields containing spaces cannot be represented unambiguously in the space-separated output. Test with disposable copies, including an empty field, a path with spaces, a rerun, missing arguments and a nonexistent file. Check that the input is unchanged and the output is in `results/`. Keep the script in the coursework root `code/`; temporary practice files belong in `sandbox/`.

This live session introduces the converter workflow. Use the shell-scripting notebook for the full practical instructions and test sequence; the lecture examples demonstrate the ideas without listing every exercise step.

::: {.checkpoint}
**Before you leave:** run a valid case, a missing-file case, a missing-argument case and a path-with-spaces case.
:::

::: notes
Time: 73:15-80:15.

Return to the recipe idea. Students should now be able to read the boilerplate.
Point them to the chapter's practical instructions and parameter-expansion
resources. The lecture has demonstrated the method; the practical is where they
make design decisions and document limitations.
:::

## The method to keep {data-timing="180"}

::: {.big-question}
What should this script do, what input will I test, and how will I know it worked?
:::

```text
create → run → inspect → break deliberately → improve
```

Shell scripts are small recipes. Small recipes still deserve tests, useful error
messages and a cautious cook (you!).

::: notes
Time: 83:15-86:15.

Close by returning to the opening question. The goal is not to memorise Bash
punctuation; it is to turn repeatable command-line work into an inspectable recipe.
:::
